764.title: Ali in the bed
764.hook: Ali sleeps in the Prophet's bed, and stays to return the Meccans' deposits (sirah)
764.howItsDone: Muslims retell Ali's night in the Prophet's bed as part of the hijra story, and point to the returned deposits when they speak of amana, keeping what is entrusted to you.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plot. Your line was: they planned; Allah planned. Which outcome did you manage to hand over? Day seven hundred sixty-four.

Night. Outside the house of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, young men from every clan are waiting with their swords, watching the door. Ibn Ishaq says they planned to strike when he came out. Inside, the Prophet turns to his young cousin, Ali, and gives him a strange instruction. Lie down on my bed. Wrap yourself in my green cloak and sleep in it. Nothing you dislike will happen to you. Today: Ali in the bed.
screen: `SWORDS AT THE DOOR.` → `LIE DOWN ON MY BED.` → `WRAP YOURSELF IN MY CLOAK.`

segments.voice: So Ali lies down where the men outside expect their target to be. Through the night they see a shape under the Prophet's cloak, and they wait. Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet went out among them, took a handful of dust, and scattered it over their heads, reciting from Ya Sin: and We have covered them so that they see not. And he passed, and they didn't see him. In the morning someone tells them he's gone. They look again at the bed, and it's Ali who gets up. But that isn't the end of Ali's job. Ibn Ishaq says that people in Mecca who had something they feared for left it with the Prophet, because he was known for his honesty. Tradition calls him al-Amin, the trustworthy. Ibn Ishaq says that when he left, he told Ali to stay behind in Mecca and return every one of those deposits to its owners. And Ali did. For days, in a city that had just tried to kill his cousin, he went door to door handing back what belonged to them. Then he set out for Yathrib himself. Consider who those owners were. The people who had left those deposits were, some of them, the same people who wanted him dead. And the Prophet's instruction about them, on the night he ran for his life, was about their property: make sure they get it back. Trust held, even then. Even toward them.
screen: `ALI UNDER THE GREEN CLOAK.` · `WE HAVE COVERED THEM.` · `AL-AMIN, THE TRUSTWORTHY.` · `EVERY DEPOSIT RETURNED.` · then, large: `TRUSTS RETURNED, EVEN THEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: return what you're holding for others. Sit, and breathe. Take a slow inventory. What do you have that isn't yours? A borrowed book. A dish from someone's kitchen. A tool. Money you owe, even a little. A favor promised and not done. Somebody's secret, which is also something held in trust. Let each one come to mind without guilt, just as a list. Then pick one you can actually return this week, and picture handing it back. Notice how Ali's job wasn't glamorous: knock, hand it over, next door. If you pray, you can ask God to help you keep what's entrusted to you. The bell holds the time.
Al-Amin, the trustworthy: what Mecca called the Prophet, the reason people left their valuables with him even the night men waited outside his door with swords. Today's word.
Your line: trusts returned, even then. Today, give back one thing you've been holding for someone else, even if you'd rather not see them. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

765.title: "The dearest land"
765.hook: leaving, he says to Mecca: you are the dearest land to me, and if your people hadn't driven me out I'd never have left (Tirmidhi)
765.howItsDone: Many Muslims quote the Prophet's farewell to Mecca when they speak of love for one's homeland, and Mecca remains the city Muslims face in prayer and travel to on pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Amin's trusts returned. Your line was: trusts returned, even then. What did you give back? Day seven hundred sixty-five.

The city that just tried to kill him is behind him now. Its leaders mocked him. Its council voted on his death. Its young men waited at his door with swords. And as the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, leaves it, the hadith keep words he speaks to it. Not to the people. To the place itself. Two companions report what he said, and both reports are kept in the hadith collection of al-Tirmidhi. Today: Mecca.
screen: `THE CITY BEHIND HIM.` → `HE SPEAKS TO MECCA.` → `HE SPEAKS TO THE PLACE.`

segments.voice: In one report, from Abdullah ibn Adi, the Prophet stands at a spot in Mecca and says: by God, you are the best of God's earth, and the dearest of God's earth to God. And if I had not been driven out of you, I would never have left. In the other, from Ibn Abbas, he speaks more personally: how good you are as a land, and how dear you are to me. If my people had not driven me out, I would never have lived anywhere but you. Listen to the two halves of that. The first half is pure love: dearest, best, how good you are. The second half names exactly what happened, with no softening: I was driven out. He doesn't pretend he's leaving by choice. And he doesn't let what the people did turn into hatred for the place. The Qur'an uses the same plain language. It speaks of the town that drove you out. So here's a man saying goodbye honestly. Grief and love, and the truth about why, all in two sentences. Anyone who has left a hometown, a country, a house they grew up in, may know the shape of it. You can love a place and still be forced to leave it. You can say both things out loud. And the story doesn't end here. Mecca will come back into his life later. Here, he says goodbye.
screen: `THE DEAREST OF GOD'S EARTH.` · `IF I HADN'T BEEN DRIVEN OUT.` · `LOVE AND TRUTH TOGETHER.` · `THE TOWN THAT DROVE YOU OUT.` · then, large: `THE DEAREST LAND.`

segments.voice: The practice: say goodbye to a place you love. Sit, and breathe. Let a place come to you: a childhood home, a city you moved away from, a room that isn't yours anymore, a street, a kitchen, a country. Walk through it slowly in your mind. The light. The smell. Who was there. Notice if there's a reason you left that still stings, and let it be true without arguing with it. Then, silently or under your breath, tell the place what it was to you. In one or two plain sentences, the way he did. If you pray, you can thank God for that place. The bell holds the time.
Mecca. Leaving the city, the Prophet told it he would never have left if he hadn't been driven out, the dearest land to him. Today's word.
Your line: grief and love, both true. Today, tell someone about a place you love and had to leave, and say honestly why you left. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

766.title: The cave of Thawr
766.hook: three nights hidden in a cave, the searchers at its mouth, and the verse: Allah is with us (9:40)
766.howItsDone: Muslims recite 9:40 and retell the cave of Thawr when they remember the hijra, and Abu Bakr is remembered as the companion in the cave.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mecca. Your line was: grief and love, both true. Did you tell anyone about a place you had to leave? Day seven hundred sixty-six.

Footsteps on rock, just overhead. Voices. Men from Quraysh have tracked the fugitives up a mountain outside Mecca, and now they're standing at the mouth of a cave, close enough that the two men hiding inside can see their feet. Inside, in the dark, are the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr, his companion on the road out of Mecca. Neither of them moves. Neither of them breathes too loudly. Today: Thawr.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS OVERHEAD.` → `FEET AT THE MOUTH OF THE CAVE.` → `TWO MEN IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakr remembers the moment himself. He whispers: if one of them looks down at his feet, he'll see us. And the Prophet answers: what do you think, Abu Bakr, of two when God is their third? That's the whole exchange. One frightened sentence, one quiet question back. The Qur'an remembers the same night. In Pickthall's translation, it speaks of when the two were in the cave, and he said to his companion: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." And the verse goes on to say God sent down His peace upon him. Notice what's not in either text. No escape plan. No promise that the searchers will leave. Just: we are not two. The searchers do leave. And Bukhari's longer account, from Aisha, shows how the hiding actually worked. They stayed in the cave three nights. Abu Bakr's son Abdullah, a sharp young man, spent the nights with them and slipped back into Mecca before dawn, so that by day he was in the city like anyone else, listening for every plot against them, and brought the news back after dark. A freed servant of Abu Bakr's, Amir ibn Fuhayra, grazed sheep nearby and brought them milk in the evening, and moved on again before dawn. So faith in the story isn't the opposite of planning. The planning is careful. It's the fear that gets answered, not with a plan, but with a question: two, and God the third.
screen: `IF HE LOOKS DOWN, HE'LL SEE US.` · `TWO, WHEN GOD IS THEIR THIRD.` · `GRIEVE NOT. LO! ALLAH IS WITH US.` · `NEWS BY NIGHT, MILK, AND SHEEP.` · then, large: `TWO, AND ALLAH THE THIRD.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit in the dark for one minute. If you can, turn off the light, or close your eyes and cover them with your hands. Let the dark be what it is. Notice your breath, and the sounds around you, and whatever worry is nearest, the way footsteps were nearest for Abu Bakr. Let it be close. Don't push it away. Then, without arguing with the fear, notice that you are not the only one in the dark: whoever you love, whoever is with you, and, if you believe, God. If you pray, you can say the line from the verse: Allah is with us. When the minute is over, stay in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Thawr. The mountain where the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid three nights, the searchers at the cave's mouth, and the Qur'an remembers: grieve not, Allah is with us. Today's word.
Your line: two, and Allah the third. Today, when worry gets close, answer it the way he did in the cave: not with a plan, but by remembering you're not alone. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

767.title: Asma's belt
767.hook: Abu Bakr's daughter Asma tears her waistband in two to tie the food bags, and is called she of the two belts (Bukhari)
767.howItsDone: Muslims retell Asma bint Abi Bakr's part in the hijrah from Sahih al-Bukhari and know her by the name it gave her: dhat al-nitaqayn, she of the two belts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thawr: two men hidden in the dark, searchers at the mouth. Your line was: two, and Allah the third. When did you feel less alone than you looked? Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

A food bag, a water skin, and no string. That is the whole problem in today's story, and it happens in a house in Mecca on the night two men are about to vanish. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr are leaving for Yathrib in secret. Somebody has to pack the food. In Sahih al-Bukhari it is Abu Bakr's daughter, Asma, who tells us what happened in that kitchen. The meal is ready. The bags are ready. And there is nothing in the house to tie them shut. Today: Asma's belt.
screen: `NO STRING.` → `A SECRET NIGHT.` → `ASMA IN THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here is the scene as Asma tells it in Bukhari. She prepared the journey food for the Prophet and her father. They looked for something to bind the food bag and the water skin, and found nothing. So she said to her father, in effect: by Allah, I can find nothing to tie it with except my waistband. And Abu Bakr answered: then tear it in two. Tie the water skin with one half and the food with the other. She did. And from that night on, she says, she was called dhat al-nitaqayn: she of the two belts. Look at how small the solution is. No miracle, no clever plan. A young woman uses the cloth already wrapped around her. The great journey of the hijrah, which we have been following for days, leaves the house tied shut with half of a waistband. Notice too where she is standing. The men are hidden in a cave. Asma is the one still in the city, still in the house the searchers will come to. The sirah tells of her carrying food out to the cave in the nights that followed, so her part was not finished in the kitchen. And look at the name she earned. It doesn't remember a speech or a battle. It remembers a quick, practical choice made with what was in reach. Aisha's telling of the night, also in Bukhari, puts it a little differently: Asma cuts a piece of her belt rather than tearing it in two. Both keep the same picture: the bag closed with her own cloth. The road to Medina did not begin with what anyone wished they had. It began with what was there.
screen: `NOTHING TO TIE THE BAGS.` · `TEAR IT IN TWO.` · `SHE STAYS IN THE CITY.` · `A NAME FOR A PRACTICAL CHOICE.` · then, large: `SHE OF THE TWO BELTS.`

segments.voice: The practice: use what you have. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind one thing you've been putting off because you don't have the right tool, the right time, or enough of something. Hold it there for a breath. Now look at what is actually around you: in your room, your pocket, your day. Ask quietly: what here could tie this bag shut? Not perfectly. Just well enough to start. If you pray, you can ask Allah for help with what is already in your hands. Let one small answer come, and stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Asma's belt. Torn in two on the night of the hijrah to tie the food and the water, it gave Asma her name: she of the two belts. Today's word.
Your line: two belts. Today, when you catch yourself waiting for the right thing, reach for the thing already in reach and tie the bag shut. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

768.title: Suraqa's horse
768.hook: Suraqa, chasing for the reward, sinks in the sand and turns back (Bukhari)
768.howItsDone: Muslims retell Suraqa ibn Malik's chase from his own account in Sahih al-Bukhari as part of the hijrah story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asma tore her waistband to tie the food bags. Your line was: two belts. What did you tie shut with what you already had? Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

A price on two heads. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Suraqa ibn Malik tells this story himself. Messengers from Quraysh came to his tribe, offering a reward to anyone who killed or captured the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, or Abu Bakr. Suraqa was sitting with his people when a man walked up and said: I just saw figures moving along the coast. I think it's them. Suraqa knew it was. And he said out loud: no, that's just some travelers we know. He wanted the reward for himself. Today: Suraqa's horse.
screen: `A PRICE ON TWO HEADS.` → `FIGURES ON THE COAST.` → `NO, JUST SOME TRAVELERS.`

segments.voice: Suraqa waits a little, goes home, and quietly sends his horse out behind a hill. He takes his spear and rides. As he nears them, his horse stumbles and throws him. In his own telling, he draws lots with divining arrows, the custom of the time, and the answer comes out against him: don't harm them. He rides anyway. He gets close. Close enough, he says, to hear the Prophet reciting. And he notices something: the Prophet does not look back, while Abu Bakr keeps turning around to look. Then the ground gives way. His horse's forelegs sink into the earth up to the knees, and he is thrown. He urges the horse up. It can barely pull its legs out, and when it stands, dust rises from the tracks of its legs like smoke. He draws lots again, and again the answer is the one he doesn't want. At last Suraqa does the thing a hunter doesn't do. He calls out to the men he is chasing and asks for safety. They stop. He tells them everything: the reward, what people are planning. He offers them food and supplies. They take nothing. They ask him only one thing, in effect: keep our matter hidden. And he asks for a written promise of safety, which Amir ibn Fuhayra, Abu Bakr's freed man, writes for him on a piece of leather. The shape of the story matters. It is not about outrunning him. The fugitives never run faster. The chaser is the one who is stopped, by the ground and by his own lots, until he gives up the chase himself. The ground did what the travelers couldn't. And the man who set out to sell them ends up guarding their secret, holding their promise in his hand.
screen: `HE RIDES ANYWAY.` · `CLOSE ENOUGH TO HEAR HIM RECITE.` · `THE HORSE SINKS TO THE KNEES.` · `THE HUNTER ASKS FOR SAFETY.` · then, large: `KEEP OUR MATTER HIDDEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: let a chase go. Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Think of something you're chasing right now. Maybe a win, an argument, a person's approval, a reward with someone else's name on it. Notice how it feels to keep riding after it. Then picture your horse's legs slowing in soft sand. You don't have to fight it. Let it stop. Ask: what if I called out instead of charging? If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you which chases to let go. Rest in the stillness. The bell holds the time.
Suraqa's horse. In Bukhari, its legs sink into the ground as Suraqa chases the Prophet for the reward, until he gives up the chase and asks for safety. Today's word.
Your line: the sand held him back. Today, when you notice yourself pushing hard after something, let the ground slow you once, and see what happens when you stop. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

769.title: Umm Ma'bad's goat
769.hook: the sirah tells of a thin goat in a woman's tent giving milk when he touched it
769.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Umm Ma'bad from the sirah literature, and her description of the Prophet's appearance is kept with the report.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Suraqa rode after the reward until his horse sank. Your line was: the sand held him back. Which chase did you let go of? Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

Dust, heat, and a tent on the road north. The travelers are hungry. They stop at the tent of a woman the sirah calls Umm Ma'bad, a woman known for giving food and water to people passing by. They ask if she has meat or dates to sell. She has nothing. It has been a hard, dry season, and the flock is out grazing. All that's left at the tent is one goat, too thin and weak to go out with the others. This is not a story from Bukhari or Muslim. It comes from the sirah and from other collections. Today: Umm Ma'bad.
screen: `A TENT ON THE ROAD.` → `NOTHING TO SELL.` → `ONE THIN GOAT.`

segments.voice: In the story, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, notices the goat at the side of the tent. He asks Umm Ma'bad about it. She says it was too weak to go with the flock. He asks: does the goat have any milk? She says the goat is far too worn out for that. He asks her permission to milk her anyway. And her answer is lovely: if you see milk in her, then milk her. He rubs the goat's udder, says the name of Allah, and prays, and the milk comes. He calls for a vessel. Umm Ma'bad drinks first, then his companions, then he drinks last. He milks again and leaves the vessel full for her. Then they ride on. See who drinks first. The host, who had nothing to give, is served first. The guest who brought the milk drinks last. Later her husband, Abu Ma'bad, comes home driving the thin flock and sees the full vessel. Where did this come from? And she describes the man who stopped by, his face, his eyes, his voice, and her description is kept with the story. A woman with nothing to offer becomes a witness. The story doesn't send her a feast. It takes the one weak thing at the edge of the tent, the goat everyone had given up on, and draws enough from it for everyone. Then the travelers ride on. Tomorrow they reach the edge of Yathrib.
screen: `IF YOU SEE MILK IN HER, MILK HER.` · `THE HOST DRINKS FIRST.` · `A FULL VESSEL LEFT BEHIND.` · `SHE BECOMES A WITNESS.` · then, large: `FROM THE DRY GOAT, MILK.`

segments.voice: The practice: share from little. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think about something you have only a little of today. Time, patience, money, energy, a kind word. Notice the voice that says: not now, there isn't enough. Then think of one person who could use a small share of it. Not the whole thing. A cup's worth. Picture handing it to them first, before yourself. If you pray, you can ask Allah to put a blessing in what little you have. Stay with that person in mind. The bell holds the time.
Ma'bad. His mother's camp fed the travelers from one weak, dry goat, milked in his name and left full for her to keep. Today's word.
Your line: from the dry goat, milk. Today, give a cup's worth of something you're short on, and let someone else drink first. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

screen: `DAY 769 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: QUBA AND THE FIRST FRIDAY.`

770.title: Quba and the first Friday
770.hook: at Quba he builds a mosque and leads the first Friday prayer on the way into the city (sirah)
770.howItsDone: Muslims gather each Friday at midday for Jumu'ah, a congregational prayer with a sermon (khutbah); visitors to Medina also pray at the mosque of Quba.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ma'bad's mother's thin goat. Your line was: from the dry goat, milk. What did you share from little? And look back at the whole week: al-Amin's trusts returned, grief and love, both true, the cave, the belt, the horse, the goat. Day seven hundred seventy.

Every day for a while, people in Yathrib had been walking out to the edge of town in the morning to watch the road. That detail is in Bukhari. They had heard he had left Mecca, so they waited, until the heat drove them back inside. One day a man up on a high place saw white-clad riders coming out of the shimmer and shouted the news. People ran out to meet them. The travelers didn't go straight into the city. They stopped first at Quba, a village on its outskirts. Today: al-jumu'ah.
screen: `WATCHING THE ROAD EACH MORNING.` → `RIDERS IN THE SHIMMER.` → `FIRST STOP, QUBA.`

segments.voice: In Bukhari's account, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stays some nights at Quba with the clan of Banu Amr ibn Awf, and there he lays the foundation of a mosque. Bukhari connects it to a verse in surah nine that speaks of a place of worship founded on devotion to Allah from its first day, with people in it who love to purify themselves. Muslims still pray at Quba today. Notice what he builds first, before a house for himself in the city: a place to pray. Then he rides on toward the town. The sirah of Ibn Ishaq says that a Friday came while he was on the way, among the clan of Banu Salim ibn Awf, and he led the Friday prayer there, in a valley, with the people around him. Ibn Ishaq counts it as the first Friday prayer he led in Medina. Some reports say the believers of Yathrib had already been gathering on Fridays before he came, so the careful way to say it is: his first Friday among them. Here is how the Qur'an names the day, in surah sixty-two, in Pickthall's words: "When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading." The day of congregation. In Arabic, al-jumu'ah, the gathering. That is what this week has been walking toward. People slipping out of Mecca one by one, two men in a cave, a belt torn in half, a hunter turned back, a woman's thin goat. Scattered people on separate roads. And near the end of the road, before he has even entered the city, they gather, in a valley, on a Friday, and pray together.
screen: `A MOSQUE AT QUBA.` · `A FRIDAY ON THE ROAD.` · `THE DAY OF CONGREGATION.` · `SCATTERED ROADS, ONE GATHERING.` · then, large: `THE FIRST FRIDAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: look toward Friday. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you are Muslim, you can plan now to go to Jumu'ah this week: picture the time, the place, how you'll get there, and what trading you'll leave for an hour. If you're not, you can bring to mind a gathering you belong to, or used to, and the people in it. Either way, notice the people you'd be standing beside. Name a few of them quietly. If you pray, you can ask Allah to bless the gathering. Stay with those faces. The bell holds the time.
Quba, the village on Yathrib's edge, where the Prophet founded a mosque first, before he had even built a house for himself. Today's word.
Your line: the first friday. Today, before you build anything else, make room for one gathering this week, and put it on the calendar. Day seven hundred seventy.

original.note: Arabic: 'the gathering', the name of Friday and of the Friday prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Friday is just the Muslim day off.
what it means: the day of congregation; on the road into Medina, scattered travelers gather and pray together.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 3906 on Quba and 9:108; Ibn Ishaq places the first Friday he led among Banu Salim; some reports say Yathrib gathered on Fridays even before he came.
